title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are: GPS in 75 Seconds
topic: How a GPS receiver works out its position by timing radio signals from satellites and turning those times into distances.
audience: Curious general viewers, teens and up, who use GPS on their phones every day but have no technical background in physics or satellites.
goal: The viewer understands that GPS works by measuring how long satellite signals take to arrive, converting those times into distances, and combining distances from at least four satellites to pinpoint a location.
tone: Friendly and curious, with a light sense of wonder, clear and unhurried
keyTakeaways: GPS satellites constantly broadcast the exact time and their own position; your phone only listens, it never sends anything back.
Your receiver measures how long each signal took to arrive, and because radio travels at the speed of light, that time tells it how far away each satellite is.
One distance puts you somewhere on a sphere around a satellite; overlapping the spheres from several satellites narrows it down to a single point.
A fourth satellite is needed to correct your receiver's cheap clock, because timing errors of just a millionth of a second would put you about 300 metres off.
mustCover: Hook: your phone finds your location to within a few metres using satellites about 20,000 km overhead
The constellation of roughly 30 GPS satellites, each carrying very precise atomic clocks
Signals carry a timestamp and the satellite's position; the receiver is passive and only listens
Travel time multiplied by the speed of light gives the distance to each satellite
Trilateration: show it first in 2D with circles, then note it works the same way with spheres in 3D
Why four satellites: three for position, one more to solve for the receiver's clock error
Close by tying it back to the blue dot on a map
outOfScope: Einstein's special and general relativity corrections to satellite clocks
Other systems such as Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou, and multi-constellation receivers
Signal frequencies, codes, modulation and the structure of the navigation message
Atmospheric delay, multipath errors and correction methods like differential GPS or RTK
Assisted GPS, Wi-Fi and cell-tower positioning on phones
The history and military origins of GPS
Privacy, tracking and who controls the system
visualStyleHints: Clean flat vector style on a deep navy space background with a simple Earth seen from orbit. Satellites as friendly minimal icons, signals as pulsing concentric rings travelling outward. Explain trilateration on a flat map view with expanding circles in distinct colours (teal, coral, gold) whose overlap highlights the position; briefly transition to translucent spheres for the 3D point. Show clocks as simple dials or digital readouts with a small 'tick' offset to illustrate the clock error. End on a familiar map pin or blue location dot. Short on-screen labels only, no dense text or equations beyond 'distance = time x speed of light'.
